Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Write $T^{\dagger}$ for the adjoint $T^*$ characterized by [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]. Fix integers $m,n\ge1$, $a\ge0$, and $d\ge\max(m,n)$. On each coordinate space $\mathbb C^r$ use $\langle x,y\rangle_{\rm root}:=\sum_{q=1}^r x_q\overline{y_q}$, linear in the first argument. Put the ancilla register before the system register in every tensor product, and let $e_0=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ be the first standard basis vector in $\mathbb C^{2^a}$. For $A:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^m$, choose as part of the data padding maps $E_{\rm in}:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^d$ and $E_{\rm out}:\mathbb C^m\to\mathbb C^d$ satisfying $E_{\rm in}^{\dagger}E_{\rm in}=I_n$ and $E_{\rm out}^{\dagger}E_{\rm out}=I_m$. The default padding sends a coordinate vector to the same coordinates followed by zeros. Set $\widehat A:=E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^{\dagger}:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^d$.

Let $J_a:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^{2^a}\otimes\mathbb C^d$ be $J_ax=e_0\otimes x$, where $e_0$ is the all-zero computational basis vector, and let $\Pi_a:=J_aJ_a^{\dagger}$. For a unitary $U$ on $\mathbb C^{2^a}\otimes\mathbb C^d$, its **projected block** is the endomorphism $B_U:=J_a^{\dagger}UJ_a$ of $\mathbb C^d$. It is not asserted to be unitary.

For $\alpha>0$ and $\varepsilon\ge0$, the tuple $(U,a,\alpha,\varepsilon,d,E_{\rm in},E_{\rm out})$ is an **$(\alpha,a,\varepsilon)$ block encoding of $A$** when $\alpha\ge\|A\|_{\rm op}$ and $\|B_U-\widehat A/\alpha\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon$. The exact case is $\varepsilon=0$. For square $A$, take $m=n=d$ and both embeddings equal to the identity. For rectangular $A$, the dimensions and embeddings remain part of the encoding data.

The equivalent projector notation identifies $B_U$ with the restriction of $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ to $\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_a)$, transported to $\mathbb C^d$ by $J_a$; it does not regard $\Pi_aU\Pi_a$ as a unitary.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.
Every linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces has a unique adjoint $T^*:W\to V$.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space $V$, the following are equivalent:

1. $T$ preserves norms.
2. $T$ preserves inner products.
3. $T$ sends every orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
4. $T$ sends some orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.
5. $T^*T=I$.

Whenever these conditions hold, $T$ is invertible and $T^{-1}=T^*$, so also $TT^*=I$. The zero-dimensional case is included.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Taking the maximum over unit $x$ proves $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

In the square block-encoding case, $J_a$ is the isometric identification of the system with $H_R=H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_a)$. The definition of the projected block in [F7] is exactly $J_a^*UJ_a$, and the exact case identifies it with the normalized target. Thus this is the stated special case.

Apply [F5] to the finite-dimensional map $A:H_R\to H_L$. For each positive singular pair, $Av_j=\sigma_j u_j$ and $\|v_j\|=\|u_j\|=1$, so [F4] and step 1.1 give $\sigma_j=\|Av_j\|\le1$. The rank-one terms in the SVD sum have the coordinate action fixed by [F6]. When $r=0$, the positive singular list and the displayed sum are empty; the kernel bases still exist by [F5].

For each $k\le r$ and every $x\in H_R$, the SVD formula, root-linear-first rank-one action [F6], and orthonormality of the $u_j$ give $\langle Ax,u_k\rangle=\sigma_k\langle x,v_k\rangle$; for $k>r$ the same pairing is zero. By [F8]–[F9], $\langle Ax,u_k\rangle=\langle x,A^*u_k\rangle$, so positive definiteness [F11] gives $A^*u_k=\sigma_kv_k$ for $k\le r$ and $A^*u_k=0$ for $k>r$. The SVD formula also gives $Av_k=\sigma_ku_k$ for $k\le r$ and $Av_k=0$ for $k>r$. Since each singular list is a basis, expanding an arbitrary vector in those bases shows that $\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n\}$ and $\ker A^*=\operatorname{span}\{u_{r+1},\ldots,u_m\}$: the positive-index coefficients must vanish because the corresponding singular values are positive and the other basis is orthonormal. The argument includes empty bases and sums.

By [F1], orthogonal decomposition gives $\langle \Pi_LUx,y\rangle=\langle Ux,y\rangle$ and $\langle x,\Pi_RU^*y\rangle=\langle x,U^*y\rangle$ for $x\in H_R$ and $y\in H_L$. The adjoint rule [F8] for $U$ therefore gives $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,\Pi_RU^*y\rangle$. Thus $y\mapsto\Pi_RU^*y$ is an adjoint of $A$, and uniqueness [F9] yields $A^*=\Pi_RU^*|_{H_L}$. Also, [F10] applies to the unitary $U$ and shows that $U^*=U^{-1}$ is unitary.

derivations.claim: For $0<\sigma_i,\sigma_j<1$, [F1] gives $\Pi_RU^*u_i=\sigma_i v_i$. Since $U^*$ preserves inner products by [F1], orthogonal projection and [F6] give $\langle (I-\Pi_R)U^*u_i,(I-\Pi_R)U^*u_j\rangle=\langle U^*u_i,U^*u_j\rangle-\langle \Pi_RU^*u_i,\Pi_RU^*u_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}(1-\sigma_i^2)$. Dividing by the positive square roots shows that the $w_i$ are orthonormal and lie in $\ker\Pi_R$. The same calculation, using $\Pi_LUv_i=\sigma_i u_i$, proves that the $\widetilde w_i$ are orthonormal in $\ker\Pi_L$.

If $\sigma_i=1$, then $\Pi_RU^*u_i=v_i$ has norm one, as does $U^*u_i$. By the orthogonal decomposition in [F5] and Pythagoras [F6], its component in $\ker\Pi_R$ is zero, so $U^*u_i=v_i$ and $Uv_i=u_i$.

Decompose $Uv_i=\Pi_LUv_i+(I-\Pi_L)Uv_i=\sigma_i u_i+\sqrt{1-\sigma_i^2}\,\widetilde w_i$. Also $\sqrt{1-\sigma_i^2}\,Uw_i=U(I-\Pi_R)U^*u_i=u_i-U\Pi_RU^*u_i=u_i-\sigma_iUv_i$, where the middle equality uses $UU^*=I$ and the last uses [F1]. Substitution of the first equation yields $Uw_i=\sqrt{1-\sigma_i^2}\,u_i-\sigma_i\widetilde w_i$, which is the displayed matrix.

If $v\in\ker A\cap H_R$, then $\Pi_LUv=Av=0$, so $Uv\in\ker\Pi_L$. If $u\in\ker A^*\cap H_L$, then $\Pi_RU^*u=A^*u=0$, so $U^*u\in\ker\Pi_R$. Every right singular vector lies in $H_R$ and is orthogonal to each $w_i$ and each $U^*u$ from the left kernel, since those vectors lie in $\ker\Pi_R$. For a positive singular vector and a left-kernel vector, $\langle (I-\Pi_R)U^*u_i,U^*u_k\rangle=\langle U^*u_i,U^*u_k\rangle-\langle \Pi_RU^*u_i,\Pi_RU^*u_k\rangle=0-0=0$, because $u_i\perp u_k$ and $\Pi_RU^*u_k=0$. Thus the listed source blocks are mutually orthogonal. Their orthogonal complement is contained in $\ker\Pi_R$, because the right singular vectors, including a basis of $\ker A$, span $H_R$. Applying $U$ preserves orthogonality. The listed output blocks are also mutually orthogonal: the left singular vectors, including a basis of $\ker A^*$, span $H_L$; the vectors $\widetilde w_i$ are orthonormal by step 1.1; and for $v\in\ker A$, $\langle \widetilde w_i,Uv\rangle=\langle Uv_i,Uv\rangle-\langle \Pi_LUv_i,\Pi_LUv\rangle=0$, since $v_i\perp v$ and $Av=0$. The remaining named output vectors $Uv$ lie in $\ker\Pi_L$, so they are orthogonal to $H_L$. The output complement is therefore contained in $\ker\Pi_L$. Since $U$ maps each listed source block onto its corresponding output block, it maps the source complement onto the output complement. These are ambient-space decompositions; the residual blocks are not part of $H_R$ or $H_L$. Each projector phase is scalar on the residual source and output blocks, so no residual component mixes into a projected singular-space block.

derivations.claim: For each distinct positive singular value $\sigma$, define $E_\sigma=\ker(A^*A-\sigma^2I)$ in $H_R$ and $F_\sigma=\ker(AA^*-\sigma^2I)$ in $H_L$. The adjoint rule [F4] and adjoint algebra [F5] make $A^*A$ and $AA^*$ self-adjoint, and [F2]–[F3] identify these eigenspaces with the right and left singular subspaces. If $v\in E_\sigma$, then $Av\in F_\sigma$ because $AA^*Av=A(A^*Av)=\sigma^2Av$. Also [F4] gives $\|Av\|^2=\langle v,A^*Av\rangle=\sigma^2\|v\|^2$. Thus $J_\sigma:=A/\sigma$ is an isometry from $E_\sigma$ into $F_\sigma$. For $y\in F_\sigma$, [F5] gives $A^*y\in E_\sigma$, and $J_\sigma(A^*y/\sigma)=y$; hence $J_\sigma$ maps $E_\sigma$ onto $F_\sigma$.

Group the positive singular terms in the odd transform by their common value $\sigma$. In any orthonormal basis $(v_j)$ of $E_\sigma$, the paired left vectors are $u_j=J_\sigma v_j$, so $\sum_{j:\sigma_j=\sigma}|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|=J_\sigma\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, where $\Pi_{E_\sigma}$ is the unique projection from [F6]. The grouped term is therefore $p(\sigma)J_\sigma\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, independent of the basis.

For the even right transform, grouping by positive singular value gives $p(\sigma)\Pi_{E_\sigma}$, and the zero-singular part is $p(0)\Pi_{\ker A}$; both are canonical projections. For the even left transform the corresponding terms are $p(\sigma)\Pi_{F_\sigma}$ and $p(0)\Pi_{\ker A^*}$. The zero right and left singular vectors may be chosen independently, but the even definitions use only these unique subspace projections, while the odd definition omits zero singular pairs. Thus all three transforms are independent of the SVD choices.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

For a gate occurrence $g=(\gamma,w)$ in a circuit on $\mathcal Q_n$, let $\widetilde U_g$ be the global embedding from [[lem-qc-local-gate-wire-embedding]]. For a layer $L_t=(g_1,\ldots,g_s)$, define
$$U_{L_t}:=\widetilde U_{g_s}\cdots\widetilde U_{g_1}.$$
For a circuit with chronological layers $L_1,\ldots,L_d$, define
$$U_C:=U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}.$$
The empty circuit and every empty layer denote the identity on $\mathcal Q_n$.

derivations.claim: Define the ancilla-controlled bit flip $X_\Pi:=H_aC(S_\Pi)H_a$, where $H_a=H\otimes I_H$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$, $S_\Pi=-I$, so [L2] makes $C(S_\Pi)$ act as $Z_a$ on the ancilla; conjugating by $H_a$ gives $X_a$. On $\ker\Pi$, $S_\Pi=I$, so $C(S_\Pi)$ acts as $I$ and $X_\Pi$ is the identity. Thus $X_\Pi$ flips the ancilla exactly on the range of $\Pi$. By [L3], each use of $C(S_\Pi)$ is one supplied call to $C(R_\Pi)$ plus one ancilla $Z_a$ gate.

Apply $X_\Pi$, then $R_z(2\phi)=e^{-i\phi Z_a}$, then $X_\Pi$ again. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$, the ancilla operation is $X_a e^{-i\phi Z_a}X_a=e^{i\phi Z_a}$; on $\ker\Pi$ it is $e^{-i\phi Z_a}$. Acting on $|0\rangle$, these give phases $e^{i\phi}$ and $e^{-i\phi}$, respectively, and both branches return the ancilla to $|0\rangle$. The induced system operation is therefore $e^{i\phi}(\Pi)+e^{-i\phi}(I-\Pi)=e^{i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$.

The construction uses two occurrences of $X_\Pi$, hence two controlled-reflection calls by step 1.1, and one variable $R_z(2\phi)$ rotation. Its Hadamard and ancilla-$Z$ gates have constant count per phase slot. Applying the same construction with $\Pi_R$ or $\Pi_L$ gives the two projector-phase operations used by the QSVT sequence; no direct or controlled reflection cost is inferred from the matrix description alone.

Let $c$ be an external branch qubit. Replace the middle rotation by its controlled version, leaving both occurrences of $X_\Pi$ unchanged. On branch $c=1$, step 2.1 gives $e^{i\phi R_\Pi}$. On branch $c=0$, the middle operation is identity and the two adjacent $X_\Pi$ operations cancel because $X_\Pi^2=I$; the system operation is identity. Thus this is the controlled projector phase. It uses the same two controlled-reflection calls as the uncontrolled construction and one separately supplied and charged branch-controlled rotation.

**Inputs.** A finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space $H$, a unitary $U:H\to H$, orthogonal projections $\Pi_R,\Pi_L$, an integer $d\ge0$, and an exact real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$. The input access contract states separately whether $U$, $U^*$, controlled-$U$, and controlled-$U^*$ are supplied and gives their individual costs. The scalar signal sequence is $U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j))$ from [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]], with its admissible polynomial pair from [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]]. A desired polynomial target is supplied with a certificate that $\Phi$ realizes its scalar polynomial; generation of $\Phi$ is a separate classical/circuit input.

**Output.** The procedure returns the finite unitary sequence below and uses its compression from $H_R=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_R)$ to $H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_L)$ for odd $d$, or from $H_R$ to itself for even $d$. No measurement or state-preparation circuit is implicit in this block description.

**Instructions.** For $d\ge0$, set the current side to $R$ and apply the projector phase $e^{i\phi_d(2\Pi_R-I)}$. For $j=d-1,d-2,\ldots,0$, apply $U$ and switch the current side from $R$ to $L$ if it is $R$; otherwise apply $U^*$ and switch from $L$ to $R$. Then apply $e^{i\phi_j(2\Pi_{\mathrm{current}}-I)}$. Thus there are $d$ alternating signal calls and $d+1$ projector-phase operations; $d=0$ has no signal call and consists only of the phase at $\Pi_R$.

For a real target polynomial, run the two phase lists $\Phi$ and $-\Phi$ in coherent control branches, with the control initialized in $|+\rangle$, and take the $|+\rangle$-to-$|+\rangle$ block. The procedure uses the reflected signal convention $W_R$ throughout. If a circuit is built through the alternative SU(2) convention, its control-dependent scalar phase must be retained as a relative phase. The exact block action, the real-part extraction, and the implementation costs are established in the separate theorem items on this page. Every phase list, inverse call, controlled call, phase rotation, and finite-gate compilation is supplied or charged separately.

Let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on a finite-dimensional space $H$, with reflection $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi$. Suppose the control-first call $C(R_\Pi)$ is explicitly supplied, together with an ancilla initialized in $|0\rangle$ and exact one-qubit $H$ and $R_z$ gates. Then the unitary $e^{i\phi R_\Pi}$ is implemented exactly by two controlled-reflection calls and one variable phase rotation, with a constant number of additional one-qubit gates, and the ancilla is returned to $|0\rangle$. If an external branch qubit is present and a branch-controlled $R_z(2\phi)$ is supplied, controlling only that rotation implements the controlled projector phase; the two controlled-reflection calls remain unconditional with respect to the external branch. In QSVT the construction is applied separately to $\Pi_R$ and $\Pi_L$; each projector-phase slot uses two controlled calls to the corresponding reflection. The access and gate costs are charged separately.

Let $C=\mathbb C^2$ be a control qubit with ordered orthonormal basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, and let $U:H\to H$ be unitary. On the control-first register $C\otimes H$, define

$$C(U):=\begin{pmatrix}I_H&0\\0&U\end{pmatrix}.$$

Thus $C(U)(|0\rangle\otimes v)=|0\rangle\otimes v$ and $C(U)(|1\rangle\otimes v)=|1\rangle\otimes Uv$. **Controlled access** means that the chosen operation model explicitly grants a call to this block operator. An ordinary call to a black-box $U$ does not silently grant a controlled call, and no query or gate cost is assigned unless the model states it.

Fix the finite circuit syntax and its complete self-delimiting binary description ([[def-qc-circuit-syntax-and-register-order]], [[def-effective-binary-encoding-and-decoder]]). For a circuit $C$, let $L(C)$ be the number of bits in that complete description, $g(C)$ its number of gate occurrences, and $w(C)$ its total number of wires.

Each clean or dirty ancilla coordinate additionally requires a declared ordered partition of the circuit wires into data register $D$ and ancilla register $A$, and a declared target unitary $V$ on $D$. In that factor order, the complete circuit unitary must satisfy the corresponding exact contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]]. For such a supplied clean contract set $a_{\rm clean}(C)=|A|$, and for such a supplied dirty contract set $a_{\rm dirty}(C)=|A|$; the notation suppresses the declared interface, which is part of the cost instance and may differ between the two coordinates. If no corresponding contract is supplied, mark that coordinate not applicable. These are counts of declared contract registers, not maxima over possible partitions. Zero initialization alone supplies neither return contract. Every auxiliary wire remains counted in $w(C)$ ([[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

The gate sequence and supports determine a finite dependency order: each earlier gate occurrence must precede every later occurrence that acts on a shared wire. A **layering** assigns a positive integer layer to each gate occurrence, strictly increasing along those shared-wire precedence relations. Gates in one layer therefore have pairwise disjoint supports. Define the depth $d(C)$ to be the least number of layers in such a layering; if $C$ has no gates, set $d(C)=0$. If layers are written $L_1,\ldots,L_d$ in chronological order, the denotation is $U_{L_d}\cdots U_{L_1}$, as in [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]].

For a family $(C_n)$ with a specified full-list generator $G$, let $t_G(n)$ be the worst-case number of Turing-machine transitions used by $G$ on unary input $1^n$. For a total acceptance predicate $A_n(x,z)$, let $t_A(n)$ and $s_A(n)$ be its worst-case deterministic transition count and tape-space use over all valid length-$n$ inputs and measured outputs, using a fixed effective encoding of the pair $(x,z)$. Any effective input description, classical preprocessing, or threshold computation has its own bit length and time/space bounds; these costs are not included in $t_G$ or $t_A$ unless the same machine performs them. The machine conventions are those of [[def-deterministic-one-tape-turing-machine]], [[def-partial-function-computed-by-a-machine]], and [[def-worst-case-time-and-space-complexity]].

If the access model explicitly supplies a named oracle gate $\mathcal O$, let $q_{\mathcal O}(C)$ be the number of calls to it. With several named oracles, record a separate query coordinate for each. Ordinary finite-basis gates, oracle calls, circuit-description length, generator time, and classical bit costs remain separate; no oracle, controlled-oracle, inverse-oracle, or data-loading operation is assigned zero cost unless its interface explicitly says so.

For an approximate task with declared rational tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$, let $\ell(\epsilon)$ be the bit length of that exact binary-rational encoding. Exact finite-gate computations have no precision field. The **cost record** consists of all applicable coordinates
$$\bigl(L(C_n),g(C_n),d(C_n),w(C_n),a_{\rm clean}(C_n),a_{\rm dirty}(C_n),t_G(n),t_A(n),s_A(n),q_{\mathcal O}(C_n),\epsilon,\ell(\epsilon)\bigr).$$
An inapplicable coordinate is marked not applicable, not silently charged as zero. This definition records the resource model; separate theorems establish polynomial bounds.

derivations.claim: The loop in [F1] executes once for each integer $j=d-1,\ldots,0$, hence it makes exactly $d$ signal calls. The side starts at $R$, so the first call is $U$ and directions alternate; therefore the counts are $\lceil d/2\rceil$ forward calls and $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$ inverse calls. If $d=0$, the loop is empty.

For a controlled sequence against identity, control each phase rotation. When the outer control is zero, every phase is the identity, so the remaining alternating signal calls cancel in adjacent $UU^*$ or $U^*U$ pairs. If $d$ is even all signal calls pair and cancel. If $d$ is odd, leave one signal call controlled and pair all others; on the zero branch that controlled call is also identity, while the one branch executes the original sequence. Thus this variant requires zero extra controlled signal calls for even $d$ and one for odd $d$, whose availability is explicit by [F3].

For a branch selector between $\Phi$ and $-\Phi$, let control value $0$ select $\Phi$ and value $1$ select $-\Phi$. At a slot with phase $\phi$ about $\Pi$, use the clean-ancilla toggle $X_\Pi$ from step 1.1 of [F2], then unconditional $R_z(2\phi)$, then a control-one-controlled $R_z(-4\phi)$, and then $X_\Pi$ again. The middle rotation is $R_z(2\phi)$ in branch $0$ and $R_z(-2\phi)$ in branch $1$; because $X_\Pi$ flips the ancilla on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and leaves it unchanged on $\ker\Pi$, the system phases are respectively $e^{i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$ and $e^{-i\phi(2\Pi-I)}$. The same unconditioned signal call occurs between each pair of phase slots, so the signal list is shared and this selector adds no controlled signal query.

There is one phase at the initial $R$ side and one after each of the $d$ signal calls, for $d+1$ slots. Their sides alternate beginning at $R$, giving $\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil$ right-projector slots and $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ left-projector slots.

Apply [F2] to each slot counted in step 2.2. The total controlled-reflection calls are $2\lceil(d+1)/2\rceil$ for $\Pi_R$ and $2\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ for $\Pi_L$, unchanged for the paired selector. A single unconditioned sequence has $d+1$ variable rotations; the $\Phi/-\Phi$ selector instead uses $d+1$ unconditional rotations $R_z(2\phi_j)$ and $d+1$ separately charged branch-controlled rotations $R_z(-4\phi_j)$, with constant one-qubit overhead per slot.

The counts above describe only the listed operations. By [F4], the cost of supplied $U$, $U^*$, controlled calls, phase gates, ancilla wires, classical phase generation, and finite-gate compilation are recorded in their applicable separate coordinates; none is inferred from the matrix $A$ alone.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $U:H\to H$ be unitary, and let $\Pi_R,\Pi_L:H\to H$ be orthogonal projections. Write $H_R=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_R)$ and $H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_L)$. The **projected-unitary encoding** (PUE) of this data is the linear map

$$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

The remaining right basis vectors span $\ker A$ and the remaining left basis vectors span $\ker A^*$. Empty bases and sums are allowed when a dimension or the rank is zero. The pairing in each rank-one map is the root-linear-first Dirac conversion of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An exact square block encoding is a special case: identify the system with the all-zero ancilla subspace and take $\Pi_L=\Pi_R$ equal to that subspace. Under the injection $J_a$ of [[def-qa-22-block-encoding]], the compression is $J_a^*UJ_a$; an exact $(\alpha,a,0)$ block encoding has compressed block $A/\alpha$.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$. For every $0<\sigma_j<1$, set

$$w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_R)U^*u_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}},\qquad \widetilde w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_L)Uv_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}}.$$

The vectors $w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_R$ and the vectors $\widetilde w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_L$. In the input basis $(v_j,w_j)$ and output basis $(u_j,\widetilde w_j)$,

$$U\big|_{\operatorname{span}(v_j,w_j)}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_j&\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}\\\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}&-\sigma_j\end{pmatrix}.$$

For $\sigma_j=1$, $Uv_j=u_j$ and the complementary vector is absent. A right zero-singular vector $v\in\ker A\cap H_R$ satisfies $Uv\in\ker\Pi_L$; a left zero-singular vector $u\in\ker A^*\cap H_L$ satisfies $U^*u\in\ker\Pi_R$. Let $M_R$ be the orthogonal sum of all positive-singular input planes or lines, $\ker A$, and $U^*(\ker A^*)$; let $M_L$ be the corresponding sum of positive-singular output planes or lines, $U(\ker A)$, and $\ker A^*$. Then $U(M_R)=M_L$. The residual ambient subspaces $M_R^\perp$ and $M_L^\perp$ lie in $\ker\Pi_R$ and $\ker\Pi_L$, and $U(M_R^\perp)=M_L^\perp$. Thus each named block is invariant under its corresponding projector, with no implicit pairing of the two kernels.

Let $x\in[-1,1]$, put $s(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ using the nonnegative real square root, and define the Hermitian-reflection signal matrix
$$W_R(x)=\begin{pmatrix}x&s(x)\\s(x)&-x\end{pmatrix}.$$
For each real $\phi$, define $Z(\phi)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\phi},e^{-i\phi})$. For an integer $d\ge0$ and real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$, the length-$d$ QSP sequence is the ordered matrix product
$$U_\Phi(x)=Z(\phi_0)\prod_{j=1}^{d}\bigl(W_R(x)Z(\phi_j)\bigr),$$
where the product is written left to right in increasing $j$ and matrix multiplication acts right to left. For $d=0$ this is $Z(\phi_0)$. This definition fixes the sign of the off-diagonal signal entry, both endpoint phases, and the product order.

The phases are in matrix order: when the factors are applied as chronological circuit layers, the rightmost factor acts first, in accordance with [[def-qc-circuit-denotational-semantics]]. In the ordered signal basis, if both coordinates are nonzero, applying $Z(\phi)$ multiplies the ratio of the second coordinate to the first by $e^{-2i\phi}$; if either coordinate is zero, that relative phase is undefined, while the displayed matrix action remains defined. This is the relative phase convention fixed by [[def-qc-relative-phase]].

For every $x\in[-1,1]$ and phase list $\Phi$ of length $d+1$, $U_\Phi(x)$ is unitary with determinant $(-1)^d$. There are polynomials $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix},$$
where $P=0$ or $\deg P\le d$ with parity $d$, $Q=0$ or $\deg Q\le d-1$ with parity $d-1$, and $PP^*+(1-x^2)QQ^*=1$ as a formal polynomial identity.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular-value decomposition $A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|$. Let $p:[-1,1]\to\mathbb C$ be a scalar function.

If $p$ is **odd**, define the odd singular-value transform by

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A):H_R\to H_L,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

If $p$ is **even**, define its right-space transform by

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{R}(A):H_R\to H_R,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{R}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|+p(0)\Pi_{\ker A},$$

where $\Pi_{\ker A}$ is the orthogonal projection in $H_R$ onto $\ker A$. The left-space version is

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{L}(A):H_L\to H_L,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{L}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|+p(0)\Pi_{\ker A^*}.$$

The odd transform annihilates the right kernel because oddness gives $p(0)=0$; the even transforms use the canonical kernel projections. The resulting operators are independent of the chosen SVD by [[lem-qa-24-singular-transform-basis-independence]].

For a finite-dimensional PUE map $A:H_R\to H_L$, the odd singular-value transform and both even singular-value transforms of [[def-qa-24-singular-value-transform]] are independent of the chosen singular-vector bases. On a positive singular-value subspace, $A/\sigma$ canonically pairs the right and left eigenspaces; on repeated singular values the transform is scalar on the whole corresponding subspace. The even transforms use the canonical orthogonal projection onto $\ker A$ or $\ker A^*$ with coefficient $p(0)$; the odd transform has no zero-singular cross term.

Let $d\ge0$ and let $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ have degree at most $d$, parity $d\bmod2$, and $|p(x)|\le1$ for every $x\in[-1,1]$. Then there is a QSP-admissible pair $P,Q$ of degree bound $d$ such that $\operatorname{Re}P(x)=p(x)$ on $[-1,1]$. In fact, the completion is exact, so for every $\delta>0$ it also satisfies $|\operatorname{Re}P(x)-p(x)|\le\delta$.

For every integer $d\ge0$, a pair $P,Q\in\mathbb C[x]$ is QSP-admissible of degree bound $d$ if and only if there is a real phase list $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ such that
$$U_\Phi(x)=\begin{pmatrix}P(x)&s(x)Q(x)\\(-1)^{d+1}s(x)Q^*(x)&(-1)^dP^*(x)\end{pmatrix}\quad (x\in[-1,1]).$$
The converse is constructive: a leading-coefficient phase peel reduces the degree at each nonconstant stage. The polynomial identity, determinant signs, product order, and phase convention are exactly those in [[def-qa-23-qsp-admissible-polynomial-pair]] and [[def-qa-23-qsp-signal-sequence]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. $$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

The remaining right basis vectors span $\ker A$ and the remaining left basis vectors span $\ker A^*$. Empty bases and sums are allowed when a dimension or the rank is zero. The pairing in each rank-one map is the root-linear-first Dirac conversion of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An exact square block encoding is a special case: identify the system with the all-zero ancilla subspace and take $\Pi_L=\Pi_R$ equal to that subspace. Under the injection $J_a$ of [[def-qa-22-block-encoding]], the compression is $J_a^*UJ_a$; an exact $(\alpha,a,0)$ block encoding has compressed block $A/\alpha$.

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

$$p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A):H_R\to H_L,\qquad p^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{r}p(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

If $p$ is **even**, define its right-space transform by

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$, and let $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ be the exact phase list in [[alg-qa-24-qsvt]]. Let $P_\Phi$ be the upper-left scalar polynomial of its QSP signal sequence. On every positive two-dimensional singular plane from [[lem-qa-24-pue-svd-invariant-subspaces]], the QSVT sequence is exactly $U_\Phi(\sigma_j)$. Consequently, if $d$ is odd,

$$\Pi_LU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A),$$

and if $d$ is even,

$$\Pi_RU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|+P_\Phi(0)\Pi_{\ker A}=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_R(A).$$

The formulas include singular values $0$ and $1$, repeated singular values, unmatched left and right kernels, and zero-dimensional singular spaces. If $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ is zero or has degree at most $d$, has parity $d\bmod2$, and satisfies $|p(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, the exact completion and phase-factorization suppliers give a phase list with $\operatorname{Re}P_\Phi=p$. The coherent $\Phi$/$-\Phi$ branch then has compressed block $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$; for a supplied uniform scalar error $\eta$, its block differs from $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$ by at most $\eta$.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, let $U:H\to H$ be unitary, and let $\Pi_R,\Pi_L:H\to H$ be orthogonal projections. Write $H_R=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_R)$ and $H_L=\operatorname{ran}(\Pi_L)$. The **projected-unitary encoding** (PUE) of this data is the linear map

$$A:H_R\to H_L,\qquad Ax=\Pi_L Ux.$$

Equivalently, its ambient-space compression is $\Pi_LU\Pi_R$, restricted to $H_R$ and regarded as taking values in $H_L$. The map $A$ is a contraction: $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$.

Put $n=\dim H_R$, $m=\dim H_L$, and $r=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. A singular-value decomposition consists of orthonormal bases $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $H_R$ and $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $H_L$, and positive singular values $1\ge\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, such that

$$A=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\sigma_j|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|.$$

The remaining right basis vectors span $\ker A$ and the remaining left basis vectors span $\ker A^*$. Empty bases and sums are allowed when a dimension or the rank is zero. The pairing in each rank-one map is the root-linear-first Dirac conversion of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An exact square block encoding is a special case: identify the system with the all-zero ancilla subspace and take $\Pi_L=\Pi_R$ equal to that subspace. Under the injection $J_a$ of [[def-qa-22-block-encoding]], the compression is $J_a^*UJ_a$; an exact $(\alpha,a,0)$ block encoding has compressed block $A/\alpha$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner product spaces,

$$(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*,\qquad (\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*,\qquad (ST)^*=T^*S^*,\qquad T^{**}=T.$$

Also $I^*=I$ and $0^*=0$.

Let $W$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. The orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]]) gives

$$V=W\oplus W^\perp$$

and associates to every $v\in V$ unique vectors $w\in W$ and $z\in W^\perp$ with $v=w+z$. The **orthogonal projection onto $W$** is the function

$$P_W:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad P_Wv=w.$$

Equivalently, $P_Wv$ is the unique vector of $W$ such that $v-P_Wv\in W^\perp$.

Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be pairwise orthogonal vectors in a real or complex inner-product space, that is $\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=0$ whenever $i\ne j$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). Then

$$\Bigl\|\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j\Bigr\|^2=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\|x_j\|^2 ,$$

the empty sum on the right being $0$ at $n=0$.

derivations.claim: Let $E_{\rm in},E_{\rm out}$ be the declared isometric padding maps in [F1], so $\widehat A=E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^*$ and $E_{\rm in}^*E_{\rm in}=I$. The adjoint identity [L3] then yields $\|E_{\rm in}^*z\|^2=\langle P_{\rm in}z,z\rangle=\|P_{\rm in}z\|^2\le\|z\|^2$. Since both padding maps preserve norms by [L2], [F9] gives $\|\widehat A\|_{\rm op}=\|E_{\rm out}AE_{\rm in}^*\|_{\rm op}\le\|A\|_{\rm op}$; conversely $\widehat A E_{\rm in}x=E_{\rm out}Ax$ for every $x$, so taking maxima over unit vectors gives equality. Thus $A_0:=\widehat A/\alpha$ is a contraction. The PUE compression $B$ is a contraction by [L1], and [F1] gives $\|B-A_0\|_{\rm op}\le\varepsilon_{\rm BE}$. Applying [F3] gives $\|P^{\mathrm{SV}}(B)-P^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)\|_{\rm op}\le4d\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\rm BE}}$.

Choose the SVD bases of $A_0$ from [F8]. For odd parity, the difference $P^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)-f^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)$ sends each right singular vector $v_j$ to $(P(\sigma_j)-f(\sigma_j))u_j$ and annihilates $\ker A_0$. Orthonormality gives, for $x=\sum_j c_jv_j+x_0$, $\|(P^{\mathrm{SV}}-f^{\mathrm{SV}})x\|^2=\sum_j|P(\sigma_j)-f(\sigma_j)|^2|c_j|^2\le\eta_{\mathrm{poly}}^2\|x\|^2$. For even parity the same bound follows by diagonal action on the right singular basis, including $P(0)-f(0)$ on the kernel. Taking the maximum over unit vectors by [F6] yields $\|P^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)-f^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\eta_{\mathrm{poly}}$.

Replace the ideal phase operations one slot at a time by their implemented unitaries. The product difference is a sum of $d+1$ terms, each containing one phase difference and otherwise unitary factors. By [F9], multiplying by those unitary factors preserves or bounds the operator norm by their norm $1$; [F7] and [F6] then give $\|\widetilde U_\Phi-U_\Phi\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sum_\ell\zeta_\ell$. Compression by the input and output projections is contractive, so the same upper bound holds for the compressed blocks. The exact ideal compressed block is $P^{\mathrm{SV}}(B)$ by [F10].

The implemented block differs from $f^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)$ by the sum of its phase-implementation, input-block, and scalar-approximation differences. Applying the triangle inequality to steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 yields $\|\widetilde B-f^{\mathrm{SV}}(A_0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\eta_{\mathrm{poly}}+4d\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{BE}}}+\sum_\ell\zeta_\ell$. The resource statement follows from [F4]–[F5]; each absent access, synthesis, data-loading, or compilation operation remains a separate supplied cost.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$. For every $0<\sigma_j<1$, set

$$w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_R)U^*u_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}},\qquad \widetilde w_j=\frac{(I-\Pi_L)Uv_j}{\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}}.$$

The vectors $w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_R$ and the vectors $\widetilde w_j$ form an orthonormal family in $\ker\Pi_L$. In the input basis $(v_j,w_j)$ and output basis $(u_j,\widetilde w_j)$,

$$U\big|_{\operatorname{span}(v_j,w_j)}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_j&\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}\\\sqrt{1-\sigma_j^2}&-\sigma_j\end{pmatrix}.$$

For $\sigma_j=1$, $Uv_j=u_j$ and the complementary vector is absent. A right zero-singular vector $v\in\ker A\cap H_R$ satisfies $Uv\in\ker\Pi_L$; a left zero-singular vector $u\in\ker A^*\cap H_L$ satisfies $U^*u\in\ker\Pi_R$. Let $M_R$ be the orthogonal sum of all positive-singular input planes or lines, $\ker A$, and $U^*(\ker A^*)$; let $M_L$ be the corresponding sum of positive-singular output planes or lines, $U(\ker A)$, and $\ker A^*$. Then $U(M_R)=M_L$. The residual ambient subspaces $M_R^\perp$ and $M_L^\perp$ lie in $\ker\Pi_R$ and $\ker\Pi_L$, and $U(M_R^\perp)=M_L^\perp$. Thus each named block is invariant under its corresponding projector, with no implicit pairing of the two kernels.

Let $A:H_R\to H_L$ be the PUE map of [[def-qa-24-pue-svd-data]], with positive singular pairs $(\sigma_j,v_j,u_j)$, and let $\Phi=(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_d)$ be the exact phase list in [[alg-qa-24-qsvt]]. Let $P_\Phi$ be the upper-left scalar polynomial of its QSP signal sequence. On every positive two-dimensional singular plane from [[lem-qa-24-pue-svd-invariant-subspaces]], the QSVT sequence is exactly $U_\Phi(\sigma_j)$. Consequently, if $d$ is odd,

$$\Pi_LU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|u_j\rangle\langle v_j|=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_{\mathrm{odd}}(A),$$

and if $d$ is even,

$$\Pi_RU_\Phi\Pi_R\big|_{H_R}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}P_\Phi(\sigma_j)|v_j\rangle\langle v_j|+P_\Phi(0)\Pi_{\ker A}=\bigl(P_\Phi\bigr)^{\mathrm{SV}}_R(A).$$

The formulas include singular values $0$ and $1$, repeated singular values, unmatched left and right kernels, and zero-dimensional singular spaces. If $p\in\mathbb R[x]$ is zero or has degree at most $d$, has parity $d\bmod2$, and satisfies $|p(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, the exact completion and phase-factorization suppliers give a phase list with $\operatorname{Re}P_\Phi=p$. The coherent $\Phi$/$-\Phi$ branch then has compressed block $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$; for a supplied uniform scalar error $\eta$, its block differs from $p^{\mathrm{SV}}(A)$ by at most $\eta$.

The projection onto $|0\rangle$ gives $A|0\rangle=\Pi_LU_\sigma|0\rangle=\sigma|0\rangle$, hence the PUE block is $[\sigma]$.
